title: Signal · Wednesday 4 November
overview: FINMA's chair unveils an AI pilot running on the authority's own hardware, Binance traces its USD 6.3 billion theft to a fake job interview and AI tooling, and an EU court adviser says chatbots can infringe press publishers' rights.

top.headline: FINMA unveils Subsuma, an AI pilot for licensing questions, running on its own hardware
top.summary: FINMA chair Marlene Amstad presented Subsuma for the first time at the Swiss Bankers Association's Digital Finance Day on 3 November. It assesses requests from the close to 100 fintech start-ups a year asking whether they need a licence, and must back every statement with a reference to the case file. It runs three open-source models on FINMA's own hardware, including Swiss-built Apertus.
top.background: It is FINMA's first use of AI to help prepare something that goes outside the authority. In a blind test, experts found quality needs larger models than the small ones tried so far; Amstad said it is too early for figures.
top.why: A supervisor now shows a pattern banks can point to: open models on owned hardware, a source for every claim, a person signing every letter. Amstad also said only about half of institutions using AI have an explicit strategy, and that accountability 'cannot be delegated to an algorithm'.
top.watch_next: Whether the next phase, on larger models, yields the speed figures FINMA is not yet giving.

top.headline: Update: Binance says fake interview and AI tool enabled USD 6.3 billion theft
top.summary: Binance's initial report on 3 November says the attack began in June, when a wallet developer downloaded a tampered AI coding tool; it replaced the device, but the team's roles had been exposed. In September a second engineer downloaded malicious code after a fake job interview. On 20 October the attackers used that computer and an internal AI tool to control wallet developers' systems, then drained the funds on 29 October.
top.background: The FBI blames TraderTraitor, a North Korean state-sponsored hacking unit, which Pyongyang rejects. Binance says it is repaying affected customers and has rebuilt the wallet system, internal AI tools and access controls.
top.why: The route ran through two things banks are rolling out now: AI coding tools and internal AI tools. Security teams will want to know who may install such tools, from where, and what an internal tool can reach.
top.watch_next: The independent third-party reviews Binance has promised, especially on how its internal AI tool was turned.

top.headline: EU court adviser says chatbots can infringe press rights but training is generally allowed
top.summary: Advocate General Maciej Szpunar gave his opinion on 3 November in Like Company v Google, the first generative AI case to reach the Court of Justice. A chatbot that retrieves an article and reuses it in an answer may infringe the publisher's right if it got past a technical barrier such as a paywall, or if the answer reuses the form of expression so closely that the user no longer needs the original. Mere facts stay free.
top.background: The Hungarian publisher sued over Gemini, which fetches web content in real time. Szpunar called the training questions hypothetical, while suggesting training is, as a rule, permitted under the text and data mining exception. The opinion does not bind the judges.
top.why: The test falls on retrieval, the technique behind many research and client tools at banks. Legal teams may want to check how those tools reach press content and how closely their answers track it.
top.watch_next: The judges have begun deliberating; judgment comes at a later date.

sources.name: Court of Justice of the EU

items.headline: Safirum launches CHF-S, a whitelisted franc stablecoin on Solana under FINMA's guidance
items.summary: Zug-based Safirum launched CHF-S on Solana on 3 November, backed 1:1 by accounts at Berner Kantonalbank and Banque Richelieu. Only identified, whitelisted wallets can hold it and only institutional investors can mint it; Maverix was first. finews calls it the first public implementation within FINMA's stablecoin guidance.
items.why: Banks get a live franc token to compare with the bank-guaranteed model still in a sandbox, a week after the Swiss Bankers Association called for regulatory easing.

items.headline: Swiss Blockchain Federation ranks Switzerland sixth of 15 on financial infrastructure, faulting FINMA
items.summary: The federation's first Global Benchmark Report, presented on 3 November with Amina Bank and law firm MME, places Switzerland behind the US, Singapore, the UK, Germany and Japan. It names FINMA's implementation, small market size and missing AI applications as weaknesses. MME's Andreas Glarner said rulings can take two or three years and some fintech licence applicants have waited three years, according to finews.
items.why: Industry pressure on FINMA's stance is rising as it pilots faster licensing answers; banks planning tokenised or digital asset services will watch which side moves first.

items.headline: Zurich city pension fund halts PK Softech migration after data theft at the vendor
items.summary: The board of Pensionskasse Stadt Zürich suspended the new administration system planned for early 2027 and will keep its current one through 2027. Test data it had sent to PK Softech was among what criminals took in the late-September attack; at worst it includes names, AHV numbers, pension data and IBANs. Federal prosecutors are investigating.
items.why: Live data sent to a vendor for migration testing became the exposure, a point for any bank or insurer planning a core system move.

items.headline: Swiss inflation jumps to 1.5 percent in October, its highest since December 2023
items.summary: The figure beat economists' forecasts of 1.1 to 1.4 percent, driven by petroleum products costing 40 percent more than a year earlier, SRF reported on 3 November. Core inflation held at 0.5 percent, and the headline rate stays inside the SNB's 0 to 2 percent range. UBS's wage survey the same day expects real wages to rise just 0.2 percent in 2027.
items.why: With core steady this looks like an energy shock so far, and banks' franc margins now depend on how the SNB reads it on 10 December.

items.headline: One in four Swiss millionaires switched main investment bank in five years, study finds
items.summary: The Lucerne University of Applied Sciences and Luzerner Kantonalbank surveyed 307 people with more than CHF 1 million in freely available assets. They hold 3.3 banking relationships on average; UBS is the main investment bank for 27 percent and cantonal banks for 21 percent. The authors partly attribute the switching to the disappearance of Credit Suisse, according to finews.
items.why: Clients who spread assets across banks can compare advisers directly, and more than a third want contact at least quarterly, which sets a service bar for private banks.

items.headline: Lloyds opens voluntary redundancy as UK banks' AI-linked job cuts spread, reports say
items.summary: Lloyds has invited staff across several divisions to register for severance, with leavers going in the first quarter of 2027, FStech reported, citing The Times. Barclays is cutting about 5,000 roles and NatWest removed 1,000 in the third quarter. City AM says Morgan Stanley has doubled its forecast of AI-driven job losses in European banking to 400,000.
items.why: Cost programmes now name AI openly, so Swiss banks will be asked for their own numbers, and the union Unite is already calling AI an excuse at Barclays.

items.headline: Intesa lifts 2026 outlook well above EUR 10 billion and lists 33 AI projects
items.summary: Intesa Sanpaolo reported record nine-month net income of EUR 8.2 billion, up 8.1 percent, on 3 November. It counts 33 AI, generative and agentic AI initiatives, about 71 percent of applications in the cloud and over 2,700 staff exits this year, out of about 12,400 expected by 2029. It says its offer for Monte dei Paschi has the required regulatory approvals.
items.why: A benchmark for European peers: AI initiative counts now sit beside staff exits and cost savings in the results, and a Monte dei Paschi deal would add scale.

items.headline: Bundesbank's Nagel says an ECB rate rise in December is very likely necessary
items.summary: Joachim Nagel, the Bundesbank president, said in Berlin on 3 November there seems to be little alternative to a hike unless the inflation outlook improves significantly, according to Reuters. It would be the ECB's third this year, from a 2.5 percent deposit rate. Investors see two to three hikes over the coming year.
items.why: Higher euro rates help European banks' margins but raise costs for clients on floating-rate credit, including Lombard loans at private banks.

items.headline: Anthropic publishes FlashProve, an open-source way to prove which model gave an answer
items.summary: FlashProve generates a cryptographic proof that an output came from a specific model, even when the lab itself runs the service. Labs would publish a fingerprint of each model without revealing its weights. Anthropic has released the specification and code as open source, TechCrunch reported on 3 November; no lab plans to deploy it yet.
items.why: Routers and gateways make it hard for banks to evidence which model answered; this points at a control that outsourcing and model-risk teams could one day request.

items.headline: Snowflake adds always-on agent bots, a governed business ontology and an AI gateway
items.summary: At Expedition 2026 on 3 November, Snowflake announced CoCo and CoWork Bots that work in the background under a user's own permissions and check in only for decisions. Business Ontology holds approved definitions for agents, and Cortex AI Gateway puts their model access, tool use and spending under one set of controls. It names Pacific Life and Shelter Mutual as users of both agents.
items.why: Approved definitions and audit trails are what bank data offices ask for first, and both now sit inside a data platform rather than around it.
items.for_your_skills: For your skills: Architecture & TOM can show Cortex AI Gateway and Business Ontology as an agent control layer option for Snowflake estates.

items.headline: Almost a third of exposed GitLab servers are vulnerable, including 48 in Switzerland
items.summary: Shadowserver counted 10,925 internet-facing GitLab instances open to at least one of two flaws rated 10 on the CVSS scale as of 1 November, out of about 39,000, Inside IT reported. One flaw, CVE-2026-97229, is being exploited; patches have been out since 12 October. All 48 Swiss instances carry the other flaw and eight carry both.
items.why: Banks self-hosting GitLab should confirm their patch status; Amstad's message to the industry on 3 November was that the time to close known holes is shrinking fast.

items.headline: Cloud waste rises again to 29 percent as AI costs complicate budgets, Flexera finds
items.summary: Firms estimate 29 percent of their cloud infrastructure and platform spend is wasted, the first rise after five years of decline, according to Flexera's State of the Cloud Report 2026, reported by Netzwoche on 3 November. Respondents overran budgets by 17 percent last year and expect public cloud spending to rise 27 percent.
items.why: Useful for AI business cases: 85 percent of respondents call spend control their top challenge, ahead of security at 82 percent.

items.headline: Update: Anthropic's compute took 58 percent of revenue last quarter, up from 48 percent
items.summary: Anthropic's amended filing puts third-quarter compute at USD 10 billion, including USD 5.0 billion under short-term commitments that cost significantly more than multi-year deals, TechCrunch reported on 3 November. Revenue per dollar of compute fell to 1.72 from just over 2. The company expects compute to remain its largest operating expense.
items.why: Token prices rest on these margins, so banks budgeting multi-year AI programmes should test a case where frontier model prices stop falling.

say_it_today: FINMA's Subsuma sets a useful pattern for any bank: open models on owned hardware, a source for every statement and a person signing every letter. Binance's report shows why that discipline matters, because its USD 6.3 billion theft ran through a tampered coding tool and an internal AI tool.
